criteria.note: The TL;DR block opens the piece and answers the celiac-traveller intent directly — feasibility, the three dedicated-GF anchors, the allergy phrase, and convenience-store baseline — followed immediately by an "If You're Celiac, Start Here" rules block, all well inside 200 words.
Title is 35 chars plus the 20-char appended suffix (55 total, under 60), description is 146 chars, the keyword appears in both, and neither restates the other's phrasing.
Headings like "What Korean Food Actually Looks Like, From a Gluten Angle", "The One Phrase That Actually Works", and the Tier 1/2/3 hierarchy carry the argument on their own for a skimmer.
Seven-plus contextually earned internal links (restaurants roundup, bakeries, phrases, BBQ guide, label guide, snacks, About), each placed where a reader would actually want the deeper page.

All five frontmatter Q/As are established in the body — the 10%-wheat bakery anecdote, the tamari sourcing caveat, the three Tier 1 venues, and the BBQ cross-contamination script — and each answer reads standalone as a rich result.

Dense with observed specifics: a dated franchise phone call, the pink-vs-green Chamsal Seolbyeong packets, a bakery owner volunteering "90% rice flour, 10% wheat flour", and a product silently renamed from "gluten-free bread" to "rice bread".

Korean terms are given with hangul plus romanisation (간장 ganjang, 어묵 eomuk, 쌈장 ssamjang), named products and brands are checkable (Goraesa, Poca Chip Original vs Onion, 쌀통닭), and the label-scan targets are enumerated as 밀/소맥/보리/호밀.

The MFDS labeling standard is linked with its in-force date, the Orion product page is linked and dated re-verified August 2026, and the secondary blogger source is linked with its October 2023 publication date and explicitly downgraded to "leads".

The piece repeatedly states what its method cannot establish ("we can't audit a kitchen", NCGS-not-celiac standard, a removed certification claim), and contains no commercial or affiliate links requiring disclosure.

findings.quote: For long-term residents, traditional home-brewed soy sauce (집간장) without wheat is the classic option.
findings.why: The body establishes the concept ("my wife's aunt makes soy sauce and gochujang at home, without wheat, the traditional way") but never uses the term 집간장 itself. Google expects FAQ markup to match visible content closely; a term appearing only in the markup is a weak spot if the FAQ is ever challenged.
findings.fix: Add the word 집간장 (jipganjang) to the aunt sentence in the 'About My Wife' section so the FAQ answer's exact terminology is visible on the page.

findings.why: The page has four sequential openers before the narrative starts — changelog note, TL;DR, 'If You're Celiac, Start Here', and a manual table of contents — and the TOC largely restates headings a reader can already see. It adds scroll depth without adding information.
findings.fix: Drop the manual 'In This Guide' list (or collapse it), since the descriptive H2s already function as the outline and the two preceding summary blocks already deliver the takeaways.

findings.why: The visible FAQ section reproduces the five frontmatter answers verbatim, which is correct for structured-data matching, but three of the five (BBQ script, dedicated venues, bread) are near word-for-word repeats of passages earlier in the body. Duplicated on-page text dilutes the unique-content signal.
findings.fix: Keep the FAQ answers identical to the markup, but trim the earlier in-body duplicates to a short cross-reference (e.g. point the BBQ paragraph at the FAQ rather than repeating the full grill-plate script).

criteria.note: The section-level "field notes, not a database" framing covers the bulk of the piece, but a small number of third-party factual assertions are stated flat without in-line attribution; none affects a safety decision.
criteria.evidence_quote: The owner has celiac disease himself, and opened 237 Pizza after years of research

criteria.note: Product names, neighbourhoods, brands and the two cited URLs are checkable, and the internal timeline (published April 2026, updated August 2026, call in summer 2025, "a year has passed") is consistent throughout.

The piece states how it knows each class of claim (visits, label reads, a dated phone call, a manufacturer page, a blogger roundup) and states what each cannot establish, with no keyword-match or name-matching dressed up as ingredient analysis.

No absolute safety guarantees; cross-contamination is addressed at every relevant point (shared grills, shared fryers, shared lines, the 같은 시설 disclaimer), and celiac risk is consistently escalated above the authors' NCGS standard rather than merged with it.

Every source carries a date and elapsed time is flagged where it bites — the 2023 blogger roundup is demoted to "leads", the 2025 call is marked a year stale, and reformulation-without-notice is stated as a standing caution.

The load-bearing fact is correct and prominent — mandatory allergen labelling covers wheat only, with barley and rye explicitly called out as unflagged — and the terms (원재료명, 알레르기 유발물질, 소맥/소맥분, 집간장) and phrases are used correctly.

The reader gets the MFDS standard link, the manufacturer product page, the source blogger post, the four Korean words to scan for, the flip-and-scan method, and the exact phrases to interrogate a kitchen — enough to check every safety-relevant claim without trusting the author.

findings.quote: The owner has celiac disease himself, and opened 237 Pizza after years of research — partly out of frustration that no one else in Korea had.
findings.why: This is a factual assertion about a third party that is neither sourced nor marked at the point of use as something the authors were told in person. It does not drive a safety decision (the Tier 1 preamble already tells the reader to reconfirm at the counter), but it reads as established fact when it rests on conversation.
findings.fix: Attribute it in-line — e.g. "the owner told us he has celiac disease himself" — so the reader can weight it as reported speech rather than verified biography. Apply the same in-line attribution to the other conversational specifics (monil2's guidance cards, tamari stocked at Lotte Mart / larger Emart / Kim's Club).

findings.quote: Yes, but few: two in Seoul — 237 Pizza (Hannam) and monil2 house (Yeonnam) — plus Cafe Rebirth, about an hour south in Pyeongtaek. Those three are the ones we trust most.
findings.why: In the body this is properly bounded by the Tier 1 preamble ("we can't audit a kitchen", "one confirming question at the counter costs nothing", "practices can change after we visit"). The frontmatter FAQ, however, is likely to be surfaced standalone in a search result or rich snippet, where it arrives stripped of those limits and reads as a flat endorsement. Not enough to withhold a point, since the body carries the caveat and "we trust most" is not a guarantee.
findings.fix: Add six words of the body's own hedge to the FAQ answer, e.g. "...the ones we trust most — still confirm at the counter, since practices change."
